node.label: Ernest Labrousse
node.date_label: Prices and incomes study 1933 · French economic crisis study 1944
node.description: Investigates differential prices, incomes and conjunctures to explain social tensions and revolutionary crises. His collective inquiry recognizes uneven sectoral movements; later historians debate the construction of his evidence and the conditions of his causal model.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Studies of prices, incomes, and the crisis of the ancien régime.
node.scope_note: Esquisse (1933), the unfinished La Crise (1944) and “Panoramas de la crise” (1956) are distinct projects. Simiand and Hamilton are retrospectively identified resources; Braudel’s appreciative use includes reservations about short duration. Perrot’s supervised strike research combines serial training with attention to lived action. Primary 1956 opening and selected scholarly reception are checked; full monographs, interview body and later mathematical defense remain unread.

incident_edges.relationship: Labrousse’s serial prices and incomes connect economic conjunctures with social structures
incident_edges.evidence_note: Braudel, p. 729, discusses price, wage, and demographic series; Gurevich identifies quantitative inquiry among Annales approaches. This does not derive econometric cliometrics or all historical demography from Annales. The 1933 title is now checked; this remains a specific French serial contribution, not the source of every form of quantitative history.
incident_edges.map_label: Labrousse: serial prices, incomes and social structure

incident_edges.relationship: Contributes conjunctural evidence and questions about uneven social crises
incident_edges.evidence_note: The primary 1956 opening differentiates sectors; Grenier/Lepetit’s later abstract distinguishes Labrousse’s experimental intentions from a narrowed serial reception. Neither source makes his programme the whole of Annales.

incident_edges.relationship: Labrousse’s conjunctures and social inquiry serve as explicit examples in Braudel’s temporal argument
incident_edges.evidence_note: Braudel names the 1933 study, revolutionary-crisis inquiry and 1955 collective programme. Praise coexists with reservations about a return toward short duration; social and economic rhythms need not coincide. The graph dates La Crise to 1944 using separate bibliographic evidence.

incident_edges.relationship: Simiand’s serial analysis is a named antecedent of Labrousse’s economic method
incident_edges.evidence_note: The scholarly obituary names Simiand and Hamilton. This group-level arrow concerns Simiand specifically, not direct personal transmission from Durkheim, and the retrospective attribution is narrower than Labrousse’s own testimony.

incident_edges.relationship: Labrousse supervises Perrot’s strike research, which adapts serial training to workers’ lives
incident_edges.evidence_note: Lacoue-Labarthe’s scholarly biography identifies thesis supervision and statistical training alongside voices and gestures. This names one formation and selective adaptation; Perrot’s later feminist programme is not reduced to this connection.

incident_edges.relationship: Later economic historians question the crisis model’s conditions and its narrowed serial reception
incident_edges.evidence_note: Grenier/Lepetit’s abstract distinguishes original experimental intentions from reception. Simonin’s opening reports causal objections and attempts a conditional defense. Different positions coexist; unread derivations and primary critics are not claimed independently checked.

incident_edges.relationship: Perrot: serial training and strike histories
incident_edges.evidence_note: Retrospective biographical evidence documents supervision and a particular adaptation; Perrot’s later feminist work is not reduced to this training.
incident_edges.map_label: Perrot: serial training and strike histories

incident_edges.relationship: Labrousse's price and conjuncture history as a model for Ouellet's economic and social history of Quebec, as Ouellet acknowledged (per Savard) and his critics named it
incident_edges.evidence_note: In-period readers; Ouellet's own acknowledgement is reported, not read. Savard (1974, ¶8, read): 'Ouellet a dit sa dette envers les travaux exemplaires de Labrousse et de Chaunu'. Paquet and Wallot (1972, read) call him 'un tenant de la position Labrousse' (p. 187) and contrast the 'position Labrousse', for which agriculture is the leading sector, with their own 'position Mauro-North' (pp. 187, 235). Tousignant (1980, p. 416) describes his method as quantitative series combined with a Weberian typology of mentalities, without naming Labrousse. The 1966 book's subtitle, 'structures et conjoncture', and Mandrou's preface are recorded on qcreq_ouellet_1966; the book is unread. Ouellet's 1985 survey (p. 47) describes 'L'histoire sociale à la façon de Labrousse' as one Annales tendency but does not there speak of his own debt.

incident_edges.relationship: Corbin explains his departure from Labrousse’s economic-to-mentalities model when subsistence practices and unreliable statistics frustrated his study of the Limousin.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own interview given in 2003, read in Christian Pierre Kasper’s 2005 Portuguese translation, pp. 14–15. Corbin describes abandoning much of the model, not every quantitative method or all of Labrousse’s work. Bertrand Gille, whom Labrousse recommended, was his actual supervisor and helped prompt the methodological change; Labrousse is not silently substituted for Gille.

incident_edges.relationship: Prost criticizes the Labroussian paradigm’s ready-made classes, explanatory reductions and restricted room for agency.
incident_edges.evidence_note: The argument also recognizes its economic explanatory gains and says the agency problem is not exclusive to Labrousse or Marxist historians. It defends historically reconstructed classes, rather than abandoning social history. Selected authorial passage in the expanded digital edition, identified by EPUB ISBN 9782757843765 (BAnQ catalog: April 2014). Read through a public third-party transcription, not a collated print facsimile. No claim that the exact wording was present in 1996; complete book and cited originals unread.

incident_edges.relationship: Charle names Labrousse among the economic readings that helped him understand publishing, imperial societies, theatre and spectacle.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own2015 retrospective78, economic-reading paragraph: this is one credited resource within two expressly plural lists, not a sole model, unique concept attribution or claim to economic-history specialization. Simiand, Vilar, Bouvier, Verley and the other named Marxist and regulation writers retain separate credit. Original works and individual transfers beyond the author’s stated uses were not freshly read. The public web-tool PDF extract was checked; direct current publisher-file retrieval returned404, so no local complete PDF or later interview pages are claimed read.

incident_edges.relationship: Roche credits Labrousse’s contextual political history and advice to avoid another regional or urban monograph in shaping his research choices.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own recollection161–163 explicitly identifies him as a pupil and describes the advice. Alphonse Dupront separately accepted supervision of Roche’s self-devised academy thesis. No sole-supervisor claim; political contexts are not reduced to a food-crisis cause.

named_group_routes.relationship: Pirenne’s comparative economic history and Labrousse’s study of economic conjunctures contribute to different parts of Annales
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The original journal title and Gurevich’s methodological account support economic history as a constituent of the project. This is a field-level contribution, not the claim that one later economic-history school founded Annales.

named_group_routes.relationship: Labroussian economic and social history at Laval
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Savard (1974) says Ouellet owed a debt to Labrousse and Chaunu; Robert Mandrou prefaced Ouellet’s 1966 book (review heading). Dechêne trained in France in the Annales milieu of Mandrou and Goubert before her Paris doctorate (1973), published as Habitants et marchands (1974) (Charron, Dictionnaire universel des créatrices; formal supervision not asserted). Linteau (1983) says social history began in Quebec in the 1960s under Annales influence but that his generation was shaped more by French and Quebec sociologists and American historians. Specific contributions to the Laval and New France strands, not an Annales origin for Quebec historiography.

named_group_routes.relationship: An agricultural crisis from 1802, joined to population pressure and a peasantry slow to change its methods, as the ground of French-Canadian nationalism and, in large part, of the 1837–38 rebellion (1962–76)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period, his own texts. With Jean Hamelin (1962, read in full): 'la détérioration rapide de l'agriculture bas-canadienne après 1802 prouve le caractère superficiel des conquêtes antérieures. Dès le début du 19e siècle, la tendance majeure se renverse' (p. 20); 'la routine paysanne, la pauvreté des moyens de transport, les habitudes de consommation de l'habitant canadien-français et l'incompréhension des politiciens expliquent la lenteur des départs et des progrès'; 'Aussi la révolution de 1837-38 apparaît-elle, en grande partie, comme une réponse détournée aux problèmes posés par l'action conjointe des tensions démographiques et de la crise agricole' (p. 31); the crisis reveals 'deux entités culturelles sans aucun doute distinctes mais offrant une grande disparité dans leur degré d'évolution', so that 'c'est moins la diversité des valeurs que la différence des niveaux d'évolution qui fut la source fondamentale des conflits raciaux'; qualification: 'Ce n'est pas que cette crise soit le seul moteur des événements de cette époque troublée' (p. 32). His 1976 restatement (read in full): the habitant, 'un paysan traditionnel', adapted positively to the export market from 1760 to 1802 (p. 115); thereafter 'le paysan, au lieu de transformer ses façons de faire, se durcit et résiste aux pressions en faveur de la rénovation du système agricole'; nationalism was born 'parmi les professions libérales' and spread 'dans les milieux paysans sous l'effet de l'apparition du problème agricole et des pressions démographiques' (p. 116). His books as quoted by critics (unread here): Paquet and Wallot (1972, pp. 193–194) quote the 1966 Histoire (p. 184) that 'l'explication ultime dans la diminution des exportations de céréales réside ... dans une défaillance de la production locale', and his 1964 CHR article (p. 291) that 'la crise agricole, par ses nombreuses implications, serait donc la toile de fond de l'aventure nationaliste'. In-period readers: Paquet and Wallot (1972, p. 187): 'pour un tenant de la position Labrousse comme F. Ouellet, la "crise agricole" est le pivot de toute l'interprétation socio-économique de l'histoire du Bas-Canada au tournant du XIXe siècle'; Savard (1974, ¶8): 'Ouellet a dit sa dette envers les travaux exemplaires de Labrousse et de Chaunu'; Bouchard (1990, ¶13): 'Dans la foulée de Fernand Ouellet et de Jean Hamelin qui, avec quelques autres, ont introduit ici l'histoire sociale, toute une génération d'historiens entreprit alors une nouvelle lecture du passé québécois'. A contribution to the Laval strand and the crisis debate, not a founding; the critics are on edge 2.

named_group_routes.relationship: Using Braudel’s remarks as reported by Dosse, Prost criticizes the marginal place that determinist social history leaves for human agency.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Specifically attributed criticism of the determinist rhetoric quoted in this passage, not a general rejection of Braudel. Prost explicitly says the problem extends beyond Labrousse and Marxist historians. Dosse is the named mediator; Braudel’s underlying statements and Dosse’s complete work were not freshly read. Prost’s separate use of Braudel’s warning about retrospective hindsight does not erase this objection. Selected authorial passage in the expanded digital edition, identified by EPUB ISBN 9782757843765 (BAnQ catalog: April 2014). Read through a public third-party transcription, not a collated print facsimile. No claim that the exact wording was present in 1996; complete book and cited originals unread.

English version: The Socialization of Quebec Historiography since 1960 (Toronto: Robarts Centre for Canadian Studies, 1988; not seen).

verification.note: Read: pp. 11–29, 38, 47, 51–52, 64–68 and the abstract, from the Érudit PDF (scanned; local French OCR; pages fixed from the running heads); the rest skimmed by name search only. Quoted: until 1963 Quebec historiography 'restée, dans l'ensemble, politique et cléricale' (p. 13); for 'Maurice Séguin, théoricien de l'École néo-nationaliste', leadership of New France belonged to the bourgeoisie, 'de sorte que la décapitation s'était exercée sur l'élite nationale elle-même'; economic inferiority as a preoccupation 'pas étranger à la montée du mouvement indépendantiste québécois', which led historians 'à négliger des secteurs entiers de l'histoire économique' (p. 18); 'Cette thèse avait été épousée par Michel Brunet dès les années 1950'; in the 1970s it 'avait besoin d'être dédramatisée'; 'Ces retouches au modèle de Maurice Séguin furent faites par Gilles Paquet et Jean-Pierre Wallot, en particulier' (p. 19), followed 'presque autant' by Robert, Linteau and Normand Séguin (p. 20); the crisis controversy began 'en 1966 à la suite de la publication de notre Histoire économique et sociale du Québec', with 'la thèse néo-nationaliste enrichie de l'idée de modernité' at its core and the peasant as '«paysan indépendant», sensible au marché et libéré'; Le Goff 'soutint en conclusion l'idée de l'existence d'une crise agricole dès le début du XIXe siècle' (p. 25); Dechêne 'n'a pu faire autrement que de prendre position' (p. 26); on the Patriotes, 'Les mêmes polarisations émergent' among Bernard, Bernier, Bourque, Dubuc, Ouellet and Ryerson (p. 51, n. 128 citing J.-P. Bernard, ed., Les Rébellions de 1837–1838, 1983); 'Fernand Dumont et Jean Hamelin jouèrent un rôle capital d'animation' (p. 67). verification.note: Read in full (pp. 115–132) from the Érudit PDF (scanned page images; local French OCR checked against the running heads). Quoted: the habitant defined as 'un paysan traditionnel ayant, au début du Régime britannique, un niveau de pratiques agricoles inférieur à celui de la majorité des paysans européens'; denies calling the eighteenth-century peasant 'morbidement conservateur' (p. 115); from the early nineteenth century 'le paysan, au lieu de transformer ses façons de faire, se durcit et résiste aux pressions en faveur de la rénovation du système agricole'; 'Si notre « habitant » a subi un traumatisme, ce n'est pas au moment de la conquête mais au moment où le système agricole traditionnel ne peut plus fonctionner comme autrefois'; nationalism born 'parmi les professions libérales' and spread 'dans les milieux paysans sous l'effet de l'apparition du problème agricole et des pressions démographiques'; Wallot and Paquet 'ont réduit notre analyse à un simple rapport entre nationalisme et malaise agricole'; their 'problèmes de lecture' made the debate 'presque stérile'; Le Goff's intervention drew attention 'sur la vulnérabilité de la thèse Wallot et Paquet' (p. 116); 'Notre analyse, contrairement à celle des professeurs Wallot et Paquet, porte sur le long terme' (p. 117); exports 1793–1802 vs 1803–12, 'soit un déclin de 30%' (p. 117); 'Si l'habitant avait été aussi sensible au marché que le prétendent les professeurs Wallot et Paquet' (p. 119); Le Goff's doubts about the revenue series 'légitimes et fondées' (p. 129); 'Le débat ne mérite plus d'être poursuivi; c'est la recherche qui exige de l'être' (p. 132). The note's n.* (p. 115) dates Le Goff's CHR article 1973 and Paquet–Wallot's RHAF article pp. 239–270; Crossref gives 1974 and pp. 185–237. Locator reconciled at release (1.138) with evidence-quebec.md §2c, which was written from the printed pages: the long-term sentence is p. 117. The PDF could not be re-fetched (Érudit bot check) to re-verify.

verification.note: Read in full (pp. 415–436) from the Érudit PDF (text layer). A review essay on Le Bas-Canada 1791–1840 (1976). Quoted: Ouellet combined quantitative series and 'la voie «sociologique» réduite au modèle weberien d'une typologie différentielle des mentalités', which 'lui a valu d'être porté aux nues, notamment dans les milieux universitaires anglophones'; 'le Fernand Ouellet de l'Histoire économique et sociale du Québec faisait écho aux vieux préjugés de l'historiographie canadienne-anglaise tout imprégnée de l'idéologie de supériorité de la race anglo-saxonne'; the approach 'qui justifiait la notion désormais dépassée du «retard des mentalités» n'apparaît plus au premier plan dans Le Bas-Canada. C'est une notable amélioration'; the crisis thesis subjected to 'un sérieux «examen critique»' by Paquet and Wallot (p. 416); 'Le choix de cette coupure n'est évidemment pas innocent' (p. 417); the 1966 book reproached the peasantry 'son enlisement dans la routine' (p. 418); 'la profondeur du fossé qui séparait Fernand Ouellet de l'école néo-nationaliste de l'Université de Montréal et de son maître à penser, le professeur Maurice Séguin'; 'Il ne saurait plus être question de porter au seul compte d'une différence de mentalités l'appauvrissement progressif de la majeure partie de la paysannerie' (p. 419); 'Lancé sur la voie de l'approche psychanalytique' after having 'raillé le schéma d'interprétation freudien de l'école néo-nationaliste de Montréal à propos du «choc» de la Conquête' (p. 423); 'Le professeur Ouellet nourrit de telles préventions contre le parti patriote' (p. 430); closing credit to 'une formalisation théorique' that gives 'une intelligibilité vivante' (p. 436, after Nicole Gagnon).

sources.title: Paul-André Linteau, “La nouvelle histoire du Québec vue de l’intérieur,” Liberté 147 (1983): 34–47; reprinted in Éric Bédard and Julien Goyette, eds., Parole d’historiens: anthologie des réflexions sur l’histoire du Québec (Montréal: Presses de l’Université de Montréal, 2006), OpenEdition, chap. 35.

verification.note: Read: a generation born about 1945 and trained at Laval and Montréal in the late 1960s wrote ‘une histoire différente’; it concentrated on c. 1850 to the present to understand industrial, urban Quebec; moved from the history of French Canadians to the history of Quebec’s whole population; social history began in Quebec in the 1960s under Annales influence, but the cohort was shaped more by French and Quebec sociologists and American historians; serial sources; Marxism challenged it but few adopted it fully. Linteau stresses a break around 1970. Checked against: OpenEdition text of the reprint (source note gives Liberté 147, 1983, pp. 34–47); Crossref DOI for the chapter. Addendum 2026-10-26: Fresh official OpenEdition HTML reprint retrieved and full 28 numbered main-text paragraphs read. Original Liberté 147, June 1983, 34–47; 2006 anthology reprint is distinct. Own ¶10 specifically credits Jean Blain/René Durocher/Claude Touchette while limiting Brunet/Séguin/Wallot influence on his cohort; ¶11 Dechêne/Hamelin concern other students, not automatic mentors of Linteau. ¶14 Harvey links colleagues; ¶19 selective Marxist challenge is not wholesale orthodoxy; ¶23 Annales influence is qualified by sociologists/American historians. Existing field routes exact; no direct personal Labrousse/Mandrou debt from a school label.

Addendum 2026-10-14: Read in full (CHA Report 41:1, pp. 17–33) from the Érudit PDF (scanned; local French OCR; pages fixed from the running heads) for the Ouellet person entry. Quoted: 'la détérioration rapide de l'agriculture bas-canadienne après 1802 prouve le caractère superficiel des conquêtes antérieures. Dès le début du 19e siècle, la tendance majeure se renverse' (p. 20); 'la routine paysanne, la pauvreté des moyens de transport, les habitudes de consommation de l'habitant canadien-français et l'incompréhension des politiciens expliquent la lenteur des départs et des progrès'; 'Aussi la révolution de 1837-38 apparaît-elle, en grande partie, comme une réponse détournée aux problèmes posés par l'action conjointe des tensions démographiques et de la crise agricole' (p. 31); 'deux entités culturelles sans aucun doute distinctes mais offrant une grande disparité dans leur degré d'évolution. C'est pourquoi le professeur Creighton a pu parler, en se référant à la société canadienne-française, de société féodale décadente'; 'c'est moins la diversité des valeurs que la différence des niveaux d'évolution qui fut la source fondamentale des conflits raciaux'; 'Ce n'est pas que cette crise soit le seul moteur des événements de cette époque troublée'; nationalist historiography's simplifications result 'à la fois du mépris de l'économique et de l'idéalisation du fait politique' (p. 32). The Études rurales version (1962) was not read.
